title: John's counsels
hookLine: short sayings for daily life from John of the Cross

lines: THE FRIAR OF THE DARK NIGHT.
SAYINGS THAT FIT IN A POCKET.
cards: John of the Cross has a reputation. He's the Carmelite friar of the dark night: long poems, dense commentaries, the soul stripped of everything. You first met him on day two hundred fifty-four, the small friar.

People who haven't read him sometimes picture someone stern and far away. But he was Teresa's companion in the reform of Carmel, and he guided other people, friars, nuns and lay people, one conversation at a time.
For them he wrote something that fits in a pocket: short sayings, a sentence or two each.

teach.h: COUNSELS: SHORT SAYINGS FROM A GUIDE.
teach.b: Counsels are advice, the kind a guide gives someone they know.
Some of John's are gathered under the title Sayings of Light and Love, and tradition says he would sometimes hand them to people written on small slips of paper. Take one.
In his own Spanish: a la tarde te examinarán en el amor.

teach.h: IN THE EVENING, EXAMINED ON LOVE.
teach.b: In the evening, you will be examined on love. The evening of a day, or the evening of a life, isn't judged on how much you got done, how holy you looked, how many prayers you said. The exam has one subject.
It fits the Bible John knew so well, the first letter of John, in the Douay-Rheims: "God is charity: and he that abideth in charity, abideth in God, and God in him."
A second counsel comes from one of his letters to a Carmelite nun, written at a hard time.

teach.h: WHERE THERE IS NO LOVE, PUT LOVE.
teach.b: His advice, roughly: where there is no love, put love, and you will draw love out. Not wait for love. Not complain about its absence.
Put it there, first, yourself. That's John at his most practical, and it's the same man who wrote the dark night.

teach.h: THE DARK NIGHT IS ABOUT LOVE TOO.
teach.b: The night, for John, is about love too: being emptied so that love has room.
The sayings are the daytime version: small enough to tape to a mirror, and hard enough to keep a reader busy for a lifetime.

how: Readers of John of the Cross often keep one of his Sayings of Light and Love on a card or in a breviary, and Carmelites read them for short meditations.

games.q: someone around you has turned cold, and things feel unfair. what does John's counsel say to do?
o: keep your distance until they warm up.
where there is no love, put love, and you will draw love out.
ask to move to another house.
games.why: in a letter to a Carmelite nun, John's counsel is to put love where it's missing, and love will come out of it.

practice: Take this saying, in the evening, you will be examined on love, and say it slowly in your head. Then look back over today, or yesterday if it's early, and ask only: where was love, and where was it missing?
If you pray, offer God what you find; if you don't, let the question sit without an answer.
